lessons.title: What happens when you type a URL
lessons.summary: The full journey of a web request, from parsing the URL through DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP to rendering, and where the time goes.
lessons.body:
"What happens when you type `https://shop.example.com/cart` into a browser and press Enter?" is the classic opening question in networking interviews. It's popular because a good answer touches almost every layer a system designer works with: naming, transport, security, load balancing, caching and the application itself.

This lesson walks the whole path once, end to end. Each later lesson in this module zooms into one hop.

## The big picture

```
 Browser
   |  1. parse URL, check caches
   |  2. DNS: name -> IP
   v
 Resolver --> root -> .com -> example.com
   |
   |  3. TCP handshake (1 RTT)
   |  4. TLS handshake (1 RTT)
   |  5. HTTP request
   v
 CDN edge --(miss)--> Load balancer
                          |
                          v
                     App servers
                          |
                          v
                    DB / caches
```

Roughly, the steps are:

1. **Parse the URL** and check local caches.
2. **Resolve the name** to an IP address with DNS.
3. **Open a transport connection** (TCP, or QUIC for HTTP/3).
4. **Negotiate encryption** with TLS.
5. **Send the HTTP request** and receive the response, possibly via a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy.
6. **Render** the page, which triggers dozens more requests.

## Step 1: parse the URL and check caches

The browser splits the URL into parts:

| Part | Value |
|---|---|
| Scheme | `https` (so port 443) |
| Host | `shop.example.com` |
| Path | `/cart` |
| Query/fragment | none |

Before touching the network, it checks a few things:

- **HSTS list.** If the site has sent a `Strict-Transport-Security` header before (or is on the browser's preload list), the browser upgrades `http://` to `https://` itself, skipping an insecure redirect.
- **HTTP cache.** If a fresh copy of the resource is stored, the browser can use it with zero network traffic. (Cache headers are covered in the caching module.)
- **Existing connections.** If there's already an open connection to this origin, it can be reused, skipping steps 2 to 4 entirely.

That last point matters enormously. The first request to a site is expensive; later ones are cheap because connections are kept alive.

## Step 2: DNS resolution

Computers route IP packets by address. A browser may use the operating system resolver or its own resolver, including DNS over HTTPS. Cached answers may avoid a lookup; otherwise a **recursive resolver** resolves the name.

If the recursive resolver has no cached answer, it walks the hierarchy:

1. Ask a **root server**: "who handles `.com`?"
2. Ask the **`.com` TLD server**: "who handles `example.com`?"
3. Ask `example.com`'s **authoritative server**: "what is `shop.example.com`?"

The answer comes back with a **TTL**, telling every cache how long it may keep it. Latency depends on cache state, resolver placement and the authoritative path.

> [!note] Measurement gap
> No measured traces accompany this lesson. The timings below are illustrative assumptions, not measurements or universal latency bounds.

> [!note] DNS is also a routing tool
> The authoritative server doesn't have to give everyone the same answer. Large sites return different IPs depending on where you are, which is the basis of GeoDNS and CDN steering. More on that in the DNS and global traffic lessons.

## Step 3: the TCP handshake

With an IP address, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443:

```
Client                     Server
  | ---- SYN -------------->  |
  | <--- SYN-ACK -----------  |
  | ---- ACK -------------->  |
  |    (connection open)      |
```

Without TCP Fast Open, the client waits **one round trip (RTT)** before sending application data. Use 80 ms as an illustrative London–Virginia RTT, not a guaranteed route measurement.

Most of that is physics. Light in fibre travels at roughly 200,000 km/s (about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum), and London to Virginia is roughly 5,900 km in a straight line. That alone sets a floor of about 60 ms for the round trip; real cables don't follow the great-circle route, and routers add a little queueing. For this assumed fibre path, software cannot beat that propagation floor, which is why putting servers (or CDN edges) close to users matters so much.

## Step 4: the TLS handshake

For HTTPS, client and server now agree on encryption keys and the server proves its identity with a certificate. TLS 1.3 needs **one more round trip**; a full TLS 1.2 handshake needs two. (The TLS lesson covers how resumption and 0-RTT shrink this further.)

The browser checks that the certificate:

- covers the hostname (`shop.example.com` or `*.example.com`),
- hasn't expired, and
- chains up to a certificate authority it trusts.

The client also sends the hostname in the **SNI** extension, so a server hosting thousands of sites knows which certificate to present. SNI has traditionally been sent in the clear, so anyone on the path can see which site you're visiting even though they can't read the traffic. **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** is a newer extension that hides it, and support is spreading through browsers and CDNs.

## Step 5: the HTTP request and response

Only now does the browser send:

```
GET /cart HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Cookie: session=abc123
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br
```

That's the HTTP/1.1 text format. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same method, path and headers in binary frames (the `Host` header becomes the `:authority` pseudo-header), but the meaning is identical.

On the server side, the request might pass through several hops before reaching your code:

| Hop | What it does |
|---|---|
| CDN edge | Serves cached content, absorbs attacks |
| Load balancer | Picks a healthy backend |
| Reverse proxy | TLS, compression, routing |
| App server | Runs your code |
| Cache / DB | Supplies the data |

The app builds a response: a status line (`200 OK`), headers (`Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`) and a body, often compressed with gzip or Brotli.

## Step 6: rendering, and the requests it triggers

The browser parses the HTML and discovers more resources: CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts and API calls. A page may make many additional requests; the count depends on the page. Many go to the same origin and reuse the connection; others go to new origins (a CDN, an analytics domain), each paying its own DNS + TCP + TLS cost.

This is why front-end engineers use hints like `<link rel="preconnect">` and why consolidating origins can help.

## Where the time goes

Let's add up a cold first request from London to a single server in Virginia, with RTT = 80 ms:

| Step | Cost |
|---|---|
| DNS (uncached) | ~100 ms |
| TCP handshake | 80 ms (1 RTT) |
| TLS 1.3 | 80 ms (1 RTT) |
| HTTP request/response | 80 ms + server time |
| **Total before first byte** | **~340 ms + server** |

Only the last of those round trips actually carries the page; the rest are setup. (The DNS round trips go to resolvers, not to Virginia, which is why that row isn't exactly one RTT.) If the server used TLS 1.2, add another 80 ms.

Now put a CDN edge in London, with an RTT of 10 ms:

| Step | Cost |
|---|---|
| DNS (cached at resolver) | ~5 ms |
| TCP | 10 ms |
| TLS 1.3 | 10 ms |
| HTTP (cache hit) | 10 ms |
| **Total** | **~35 ms** |

In these illustrative assumptions the total is about ten times lower, combining a nearer endpoint, a faster DNS lookup and a cache hit. Note the hidden assumption: the edge had the response cached. On a miss, the edge must still fetch from Virginia, adding one 80 ms trip over a connection it keeps warm, so the total is closer to 115 ms. That's still three times better than going direct.

Most of this module is about techniques that shrink, skip or move these round trips.

> [!tip] Interview framing
> Don't recite every step at equal depth. Walk the path briefly, then say "the expensive parts are the round trips: DNS, TCP and TLS. Here's how we cut them: caching, connection reuse, TLS 1.3/QUIC and edge termination." That shows you know what matters.

## Failure modes along the path

Every hop can fail, and each failure looks different to the user:

- **DNS failure:** "server not found" (`NXDOMAIN` or timeout). The 2016 Dyn attack took down Twitter, GitHub and others this way.
- **TCP failure:** "connection refused" (the host answered with a reset because nothing is listening on that port) or a timeout (a firewall silently dropping packets, or a dead host). Refused is fast; a timeout can hang for many seconds, which is why client connect timeouts matter.
- **TLS failure:** certificate warnings, often from an expired certificate.
- **HTTP failure:** a `502 Bad Gateway` reports an invalid upstream response; a `504 Gateway Timeout` reports an upstream timeout. Inspect backend health, the network and proxy configuration; the status alone does not prove which component is faulty.

Knowing which layer produced an error is the first step in debugging production incidents.

## Key takeaways

- A request goes: URL parse → caches → DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP → server stack → render.
- The fixed cost of a new connection is several round trips, and RTT is bounded by distance and the speed of light.
- Connection reuse, DNS caching, TLS 1.3 and serving from the edge each remove or shorten round trips.
- DNS answers can differ per client, which makes DNS a traffic-routing tool, not just a phone book.
- Error type (DNS, connection refused, TLS, 502/504) tells you which hop failed.

questions.prompt: Assume HTTPS over TCP, no cached DNS answer or open connection, and no TCP Fast Open or TLS early data. What is the normal order?

options.text: TCP handshake → DNS lookup → TLS handshake → HTTP request
options.explanation: TCP needs a destination IP address to send the SYN to, so it can't happen before DNS has turned the name into an IP.

options.text: DNS lookup → TLS handshake → TCP handshake → HTTP request
options.explanation: TLS (over TCP) runs inside an established TCP connection; there's nowhere to send the ClientHello until TCP is open.

options.text: DNS lookup → HTTP request → TLS handshake → TCP handshake
options.explanation: For HTTPS the HTTP request is encrypted, so it can only be sent after TLS has established keys; it can't come before the transport and security layers exist.

options.text: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request
options.explanation: Correct. The name must be resolved first, then a TCP connection opened to that IP, then TLS negotiated over it, and only then can the encrypted HTTP request be sent.

questions.workedExample:
Work from dependencies:

1. TCP needs an **IP address** → DNS must come first.
2. TLS messages travel **over** the TCP connection → TCP comes before TLS.
3. The HTTP request is **encrypted with TLS keys** → TLS comes before HTTP.

So: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP. (With HTTP/3, QUIC merges the transport and TLS handshakes into one, but DNS still comes first.)

questions.prompt: A user in London fetches a page from a single server in Virginia. RTT is 80 ms. DNS is already cached, and the server takes 20 ms to generate the response. Using TLS 1.3 on a brand-new connection, roughly how long until the first byte of the response arrives?

options.text: About 100 ms
options.explanation: This counts only one round trip plus server time, as if the connection were already open. A new connection must first pay for the TCP and TLS handshakes.

options.text: About 260 ms
options.explanation: Correct. TCP (1 RTT = 80 ms) + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT = 80 ms) + request/response (1 RTT = 80 ms) + 20 ms server time = 260 ms.

options.text: About 340 ms
options.explanation: This includes an uncached DNS lookup (~80–100 ms) or a TLS 1.2 two-RTT handshake. The question says DNS is cached and TLS 1.3 needs only one round trip.

options.text: About 180 ms
options.explanation: This counts two round trips plus server time, so it has dropped one of TCP, TLS or the request itself. All three are needed on a new connection.

questions.workedExample:
Count the round trips on a cold connection:

| Step | RTTs | Time |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | 0 (cached) | 0 ms |
| TCP SYN/SYN-ACK | 1 | 80 ms |
| TLS 1.3 | 1 | 80 ms |
| GET + response | 1 | 80 ms |
| Server work | - | 20 ms |

Total = 80 + 80 + 80 + 20 = **260 ms**. Notice that 160 ms of that is setup. On a reused connection the same request would take only 100 ms.

questions.prompt: Users report ~900 ms page loads from Sydney and ~150 ms from New York. Your only servers are in us-east-1 and HTML is uncacheable. Traces show that the Sydney delay is dominated by connection-setup round trips; servers are not saturated and transfer time is negligible. Which listed change directly reduces that delay?

options.text: Putting a CDN in front so TCP and TLS terminate at a Sydney edge, with the edge keeping warm connections to the origin
options.explanation: Correct. The handshakes now cost a ~10 ms RTT instead of ~200 ms, and the edge reuses a long-lived connection to Virginia, so only the request itself crosses the Pacific. Even uncacheable HTML benefits.

options.text: Doubling the number of app servers in us-east-1
options.explanation: More servers help if they're overloaded, but New York is fast, so server capacity isn't the bottleneck. Sydney's problem is the ~200 ms RTT, which extra servers in Virginia don't change.

options.text: Upgrading the database to a larger instance
options.explanation: Database time is the same for both cities, and New York is already fast. The extra ~750 ms in Sydney comes from distance, not query time.

options.text: Switching from gzip to Brotli compression
options.explanation: Brotli shaves a few kilobytes, which helps bandwidth, but the delay here is dominated by round trips, not bytes. A smaller body still pays the same 3–4 trans-Pacific RTTs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the cities: the supplied traces establish that connection-setup round trips dominate.
2. Sydney to Virginia RTT ≈ 200 ms. A cold page load is DNS + TCP + TLS + request ≈ 4 RTT ≈ 800 ms, which matches the ~900 ms observed.
3. With a Sydney edge: assume DNS costs 10 ms and TCP and TLS each cost 10 ms. The edge forwards the request over an already-open connection to the origin: 1 × 200 ms.
4. New total ≈ 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 (client–edge request/response) + 200 + server time ≈ **250 ms**.

Adding servers, a bigger database or better compression doesn't touch the round-trip count, which is where the time goes.

questions.prompt: Which of these let a browser skip one or more network round trips on a later visit to the same site? Select all that apply.

options.text: A fresh copy of the resource in the browser's HTTP cache
options.explanation: Correct. If the cached response is still fresh, the browser uses it without any network request at all: no DNS, TCP, TLS or HTTP round trips.

options.text: An HSTS entry for the domain
options.explanation: Correct. HSTS makes the browser go straight to HTTPS, skipping the round trip(s) of an `http://` request that would only return a 301 redirect to `https://`.

options.text: Reusing a kept-alive connection to the origin
options.explanation: Correct. A reused connection has already done DNS, TCP and TLS, so the next request costs just one round trip.

options.text: Setting a longer `Content-Length` header
options.explanation: `Content-Length` just tells the receiver how big the body is. It has no effect on handshakes or caching, so it saves no round trips.

options.text: A cached DNS answer still within its TTL
options.explanation: Correct. A cached answer lets the client skip the resolver queries entirely, saving anything from a few ms to over 100 ms.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each round trip and ask what removes it:

- **DNS** → cached answer within TTL.
- **http→https redirect** → HSTS.
- **TCP + TLS** → reuse an existing connection.
- **The whole request** → a fresh HTTP cache entry.

`Content-Length` describes a body; it doesn't remove any step. So the answer is the cache, HSTS, connection reuse and DNS caching.

questions.prompt: During an incident, users get `502 Bad Gateway` from `api.example.com`. Your setup is CDN → load balancer → app servers. What does the 502 tell you most directly?

options.text: DNS for `api.example.com` is broken
options.explanation: If DNS were broken the client couldn't reach anything, and would see a 'server not found' error rather than an HTTP status. Getting a 502 means DNS, TCP and TLS to the first hop all worked.

options.text: The client sent a malformed request
options.explanation: Malformed client requests produce 4xx errors such as 400 Bad Request. A 5xx code means the problem is on the server side.

options.text: The TLS certificate has expired
options.explanation: An expired certificate on the edge makes the browser abort the handshake with a certificate error, before any HTTP status exists. The user wouldn't see a 502 page.

options.text: A proxy in the chain is up, but got an invalid or no response from the server behind it
options.explanation: Correct. 502 is generated by a gateway or proxy (the CDN or load balancer) when its upstream fails, for example app servers crashing, refusing connections or closing them mid-response.

questions.workedExample:
1. The user received an **HTTP status**, so DNS, TCP and TLS to the first hop succeeded.
2. 5xx means server side; specifically, **502 and 504 come from intermediaries**.
3. 502 = the upstream gave a bad or no response; 504 = the upstream was too slow.
4. So check the hop *behind* the one reporting it: is the load balancer seeing healthy targets? Are app servers crashing or restarting?

This layer-by-layer reasoning narrows an incident fast.

questions.prompt: A page loads resources from three additional unrelated origins. Assume they cannot coalesce connections, RTT to each is 40 ms, each DNS lookup independently takes 40 ms, and each uses a new TLS 1.3/TCP connection without early data or retry. What setup cost does each origin add, and what helps?

options.text: The browser has to download the TLS certificate chain three extra times, which costs about 1 MB
options.explanation: Certificate chains are a few kilobytes, not megabytes. The cost is round-trip latency for each handshake, not certificate bandwidth.

options.text: There's no extra cost because HTTP/2 multiplexes all origins over one connection
options.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests within one connection to **one origin**. It can't carry requests for unrelated hostnames on different servers.

options.text: Each origin needs its own DNS + TCP + TLS (about 3 RTT ≈ 120 ms); consolidate onto fewer origins or use `preconnect` hints
options.explanation: Correct. Connections can't be shared across different hostnames (without certificate and IP coalescing), so each new origin pays its own setup. Fewer origins or early `preconnect` hides or removes that cost.

options.text: Browsers block third-party scripts, so the scripts never load
options.explanation: Browsers block some third-party cookies and trackers, not scripts in general. The question is about latency, and these resources do load.

questions.workedExample:
1. A new origin = new hostname = new DNS lookup (~1 RTT to a resolver), a new TCP handshake (1 RTT) and a new TLS handshake (1 RTT).
2. That's ≈ 3 × 40 = **120 ms** of setup per origin before its first request.
3. The browser does these in parallel, but they start only once the HTML has been parsed far enough to discover them, so they sit on the critical path.
4. Fixes: self-host fonts and scripts on the main origin (it's reusing a warm connection), or add `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.cdn-a.net">` so the setup starts while the HTML is still downloading.

questions.prompt: Your product team wants a 100 ms time-to-first-byte target for users in Mumbai. Your origin is in Frankfurt (RTT ≈ 120 ms), and responses are personalised and uncacheable. What is the honest assessment?

options.text: Achievable by tuning the app server to respond in under 10 ms
options.explanation: Even a 0 ms server can't beat physics: at least one 120 ms round trip to Frankfurt is needed to get personalised data, which already exceeds 100 ms.

options.text: Not achievable from Frankfurt; you need compute and data closer to Mumbai (e.g. an Indian region), and an edge only partly helps
options.explanation: Correct. An edge removes the handshake RTTs, but the uncacheable request still needs one 120 ms trip to the origin. Meeting 100 ms means moving the origin, or the data it needs, nearer to the users.

options.text: Achievable with TLS 1.3 0-RTT alone
options.explanation: 0-RTT removes the TLS round trip on resumption, but the request still has to travel to Frankfurt and back (120 ms), so it can't reach 100 ms on its own.

options.text: Achievable by switching to UDP
options.explanation: Changing transport can remove handshake round trips, but the request/response still has to cross the 120 ms path. UDP doesn't make light travel faster.

questions.workedExample:
1. Assume each response requires a round trip to Frankfurt, with a fixed 120 ms RTT. That alone exceeds the 100 ms target.
2. A Mumbai edge with 5 ms client RTT, a warm 120 ms origin path and new TCP/TLS connection takes 5 + 5 + 5 + 120 + server time = 135 ms plus server time.
3. Meeting the target requires changing the dependency or placing the necessary compute/data closer. Actual routing improvements could also change the assumed RTT; 120 ms is a scenario input, not a universal physical constant.

questions.prompt: Assume a client starts with an explicit `http://bank.example.com/` URL and has no HTTPS-first upgrading, HTTPS DNS upgrade, cached/inherited HSTS policy or preload entry. The server redirects HTTP to HTTPS and sends HSTS over HTTPS. What happens on the first visit?

options.text: The browser goes straight to HTTPS because the site supports HSTS
options.explanation: HSTS itself cannot upgrade this request because this client has no applicable policy. Other browser features can prefer HTTPS, but the question explicitly excludes them.

options.text: The browser sends a plain `http://` request, gets a redirect to `https://`, and only then learns the HSTS policy for future visits
options.explanation: Correct. The first request goes out unencrypted and the redirect costs an extra round trip (or more). That first hop is also the window an on-path attacker can exploit, which is exactly what the preload list closes.

options.text: The connection fails because HSTS forbids plain HTTP entirely
options.explanation: HSTS tells a browser that has already seen the policy to refuse plain HTTP. It can't affect a browser that has never received it.

options.text: The DNS resolver upgrades the request to HTTPS
options.explanation: DNS only maps names to addresses; it doesn't rewrite URL schemes. (An `HTTPS` DNS record can hint that a site supports HTTPS, but that's a browser decision, not the resolver's.)

questions.workedExample:
1. HSTS is learnt from a response header, so the browser must receive one HTTPS response first.
2. First visit: the specified client starts with the explicit `http://` URL, connects to port 80 and sends the request in the clear.
3. The server replies `301` to `https://bank.example.com/`: one wasted round trip, plus a new TCP connection to port 443.
4. Over HTTPS, the response carries `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=...`. From now on the browser upgrades by itself.
5. To protect even the first visit, submit the domain to the **HSTS preload list**, which ships inside browsers.

questions.prompt: Your mobile app reports that connecting to `api.example.com` sometimes *hangs for about 20 seconds* and then fails, rather than failing instantly. DNS resolves correctly. Which explanation fits the symptom best?

options.text: Nothing is listening on port 443, so the server refuses the connection
options.explanation: A host with nothing listening replies at once with a TCP reset, which the client reports immediately as 'connection refused'. That's fast, not a 20-second hang.

options.text: The certificate has expired
options.explanation: Certificate checks happen after TCP connects, during the TLS handshake, and fail quickly with a certificate error. They don't cause a long silent wait before connecting.

options.text: The server returned `504 Gateway Timeout`
options.explanation: A 504 is an HTTP response, which means TCP and TLS already succeeded. The symptom here is failing to connect at all.

options.text: SYN packets are being silently dropped (a firewall or security group rule, or a dead host), so the client keeps retransmitting until its connect timeout expires
options.explanation: Correct. With no reply at all, the client's TCP stack retries the SYN with growing gaps (roughly 1 s, 2 s, 4 s...) until the app's connect timeout fires. Silence means drop; an instant failure means refusal.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the two TCP failure shapes:

| Symptom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Instant 'refused' | Host replied with RST |
| Long hang, timeout | No reply at all |

1. DNS is fine and the failure happens *before* TLS, so it's at the TCP layer.
2. A hang means SYNs vanish: a firewall rule dropping traffic, a host that's down, or a route that black-holes packets.
3. The client retransmits the SYN with exponential backoff until its connect timeout.
4. Fixes: check security groups and network ACLs, and set a short client connect timeout (a few seconds) so the app fails fast and can retry elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A London user requests an uncacheable page through a CDN edge in London (RTT 10 ms). The origin is in Virginia (edge-to-origin RTT 80 ms) and the edge already holds a warm connection to it. DNS is cached, TLS 1.3 is used, and the origin takes 20 ms. Roughly what is the time to first byte on a new user connection?

options.text: About 35 ms
options.explanation: That's the cache-hit case from the lesson. On a miss, the edge still has to fetch the page from Virginia, which costs at least one 80 ms round trip.

options.text: About 340 ms
options.explanation: That's going direct to Virginia with an uncached DNS lookup. The handshakes here happen with the nearby edge, not with Virginia.

options.text: About 130 ms
options.explanation: Correct. TCP 10 + TLS 10 + request to the edge 10 + edge-to-origin round trip 80 + server 20 = 130 ms.

options.text: About 290 ms
options.explanation: This charges full handshakes to Virginia as well. Because the edge reuses a warm connection, only the request itself crosses the Atlantic.

questions.workedExample:
Split the path into the short hop and the long hop:

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| TCP to edge | 10 ms |
| TLS 1.3 at edge | 10 ms |
| Request to edge | 10 ms |
| Edge to origin (warm) | 80 ms |
| Origin work | 20 ms |
| **Total** | **130 ms** |

Direct, it would be 3 × 80 + 20 = 260 ms. The edge halves it by moving the handshakes, but it can't remove the one trip to wherever the data lives.

questions.prompt: Assume a 17,000 km fibre path at 200,000 km/s. What propagation floor does that imply for RTT and for four sequential round trips over this same path?

options.text: About 57 ms, so a well-tuned server could serve Sydney from London quickly
options.explanation: 57 ms is the one-way time for light in a *vacuum* (17,000 / 300,000 s). Fibre is slower, and a round trip goes there and back.

options.text: About 85 ms, so three round trips fit in a quarter of a second
options.explanation: 85 ms is the one-way time in fibre. A round trip doubles it.

options.text: About 340 ms, because each round trip crosses the distance four times
options.explanation: A round trip crosses the distance twice (there and back), not four times.

options.text: About 170 ms for the assumed fibre path, so four sequential trips over it require at least 680 ms before other delays
options.explanation: Correct. One-way: 17,000 / 200,000 = 85 ms; round trip ≈ 170 ms. Cables don't follow the great circle, so real RTTs are higher still. Only moving servers or edges closer beats this.

questions.workedExample:
1. One way: 17,000 / 200,000 s = 85 ms.
2. Round trip: 170 ms before additional queueing or route distance.
3. Four sequential trips over that same path take at least 680 ms. This does not automatically describe a cold HTTPS request: DNS may use a nearby resolver, while a normal TCP/TLS1.3 request needs three origin round trips.
4. Protocol changes reduce trip counts; endpoint placement, physical route and transmission medium affect propagation time.

questions.prompt: A network operator can inspect your decrypted IP packets on café Wi-Fi. You access `https://shop.example.com/cart` using plain UDP DNS, no VPN/proxy and no ECH. What can this passive observer learn directly? Select all that apply.

options.text: The IP address of the server you connect to
options.explanation: Correct. IP headers must be readable for packets to be routed, so the destination address is always visible.

options.text: The path `/cart` and your session cookie
options.explanation: These are inside the encrypted HTTP request. TLS hides the method, path, headers, cookies and body.

options.text: The hostname `shop.example.com`, from the DNS query
options.explanation: Correct. Classic DNS over UDP port 53 is unencrypted, so the query and answer are visible. DoH or DoT would hide this hop.

options.text: The hostname `shop.example.com`, from the TLS ClientHello
options.explanation: Correct. Without ECH, the SNI extension carries the hostname in the clear so the server can choose a certificate.

options.text: The exact prices on the page
options.explanation: The response body is encrypted. An observer sees only its approximate size and timing.

questions.workedExample:
1. In this scenario the observer sees destination IP headers; a VPN would instead expose its outer endpoint.
2. Plain UDP DNS reveals the queried hostname.
3. Without ECH, SNI reveals the hostname again.
4. TLS encrypts the HTTP path, cookies and body. Timing, size and destination IP can still leak information; encrypted DNS plus ECH does not guarantee site anonymity.

lessons.summary: How DNS resolution really works, the record types you'll use, how TTLs and caching shape failover, and how DNS doubles as a load balancer.
lessons.body:
DNS (the Domain Name System) maps names like `api.example.com` to the addresses and services behind them. It's one of the oldest and largest distributed databases on the internet, and it's on the critical path of almost every request.

For a system designer, DNS matters for three reasons:

- It adds latency to the first request.
- Its **caching** decides how fast you can move traffic during a failover.
- It's a cheap, global **load-balancing and routing layer**.

## The cast of characters

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| Stub resolver | Library in your OS; asks one resolver |
| Recursive resolver | Does the legwork, caches answers |
| Root servers | Know who runs each TLD |
| TLD servers | Know who runs each domain |
| Authoritative server | Holds the actual records |

There are 13 root server *identities* (a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net), run by 12 independent organisations. Each identity is served from many sites via **anycast**, and together they are deployed at many locations worldwide (the site count changes over time), so "13 root servers" is a naming detail, not a capacity limit. (The number 13 comes from fitting all their addresses into one small, original-size DNS response.)

## A full resolution, step by step

```
App -> Stub -> Recursive resolver
                 |
   1 "www.example.com?"   -> Root
     "ask .com servers"   <-
   2 "www.example.com?"   -> .com TLD
     "ask ns1.example.com"<-
   3 "www.example.com?"   -> ns1.example
     "A 192.0.2.10"       <-
                 |
          cache + return
```

1. The recursive resolver asks a **root** server, which replies with a *referral* to the `.com` servers.
2. It asks a **`.com`** server, which refers it to `example.com`'s name servers (from the `NS` records registered with the registrar).
3. It asks the **authoritative** server, which returns the answer.

The recursive resolver does **iterative** queries (it follows referrals itself); the stub makes a single **recursive** query ("give me the final answer"). In practice, the root and TLD referrals are almost always cached, so most lookups need only step 3 or are answered entirely from cache.

DNS normally runs over **UDP port 53**: one small packet each way, no handshake. If an answer is too big for the UDP size the client advertised (EDNS(0) lets clients advertise larger buffers; around 1,232 bytes is the common safe default since DNS Flag Day 2020, to avoid IP fragmentation), the server sets the *truncated* flag and the client retries over **TCP**. TCP support is mandatory, not optional (RFC 7766), and matters for DNSSEC-signed answers. DNS is also increasingly carried over TLS (DoT) or HTTPS (DoH) for privacy.

## Record types you'll actually use

| Type | Maps to | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| `A` | IPv4 address | `api` → 203.0.113.10 |
| `AAAA` | IPv6 address | `api` → 2001:db8::10 |
| `CNAME` | Another name | `www` → `shop.cdn.net` |
| `NS` | Name servers | Delegating a zone |
| `MX` | Mail servers | Email for the domain |
| `TXT` | Free text | SPF, domain verification |
| `SRV` | Host + port | Service discovery |
| `CAA` | Allowed CAs | Who may issue certs |

A few gotchas worth knowing:

- **A `CNAME` can't sit at the zone apex** (`example.com` itself), because the apex must also hold `NS` and `SOA` records and a CNAME cannot coexist with ordinary data at the same owner name (DNSSEC-related records have specific exceptions). Providers work around this with "ALIAS" or "ANAME" records (Route 53 calls them alias records), which resolve the target server-side and return A records.
- **CNAME chains cost lookups.** `www` → `shop.cdn.net` → `edge.cdn.net` → IP may need extra queries if the intermediate names aren't cached.
- **`HTTPS`/`SVCB` records** (RFC 9460) are newer: they can tell a browser up front that a site supports HTTP/3, saving a round trip of discovery.

## TTLs and caching

Every record carries a **TTL** (time to live) in seconds. Any resolver can cache the answer for that long.

```
www.example.com. 300 IN A 203.0.113.10
                 ^^^
                 cache for 5 minutes
```

Caching is why DNS scales: a popular resolver answers millions of queries for `google.com` from memory. But it creates the central DNS trade-off:

| Short TTL (30–60 s) | Long TTL (hours–days) |
|---|---|
| Fast failover and changes | Slow to change |
| More queries, more latency | Fewer queries, faster |
| More load on your DNS | Resilient if DNS is down |

**Negative answers are cached too.** If a name doesn't exist (`NXDOMAIN`), resolvers cache that for the zone's negative TTL: the smaller of the `SOA` record's own TTL and its `MINIMUM` field (RFC 2308). If you query a name before creating it, clients may keep getting "doesn't exist" for a while after you add it.

**The TTL counts down in caches.** A resolver that cached a 300 s record 200 s ago hands it out with a TTL of 100. So the TTL a client sees is the *remaining* lifetime, and every cache downstream of it expires at the same moment, not 300 s after it asked.

> [!warning] TTLs are a request, not a guarantee
> Some resolvers enforce a minimum TTL, some clients (old JVMs, some mobile OSes, connection pools) cache much longer than told, and long-lived TCP connections never re-resolve at all. Many resolvers also implement **serve-stale** (RFC 8767): if the authoritative servers are unreachable, they keep answering from expired cache entries rather than failing. That's good for resilience, but it's another way old answers outlive their TTL. Plan for a long tail: after a DNS change, a small percentage of traffic often keeps hitting the old address for hours.

### The TTL-lowering playbook

If you're migrating a service to new IPs:

1. Days before, lower the TTL from, say, 86,400 s to 60 s.
2. Wait at least the *old* TTL (24 hours) so normally expiring caches no longer retain an answer with the old long TTL; caches need not refresh until queried.
3. Change the record. Most clients move within a minute or two.
4. Keep the old servers running until traffic drains.
5. Raise the TTL again.

Skipping step 2 is a classic mistake: caches still holding the 24-hour record won't look again for up to a day.

## DNS as a load-balancing tool

The authoritative server decides what to return, and it can be clever about it.

### Round-robin DNS

Return several `A` records and rotate their order:

```
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.10
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.11
api.example.com. 60 A 203.0.113.12
```

Clients usually try the first, so load spreads roughly evenly. (Not always: some operating systems sort addresses using RFC 6724 rules, which can undo the rotation and favour one IP.) It's simple, but crude:

- **No health awareness.** Plain DNS keeps handing out a dead server's IP.
- **Uneven.** One big corporate resolver may send thousands of users to the same IP.
- **Slow to react,** because of caching.

### Smarter answers

Managed DNS services (Route 53, Azure Traffic Manager, NS1, Cloudflare) layer policies on top:

- **Health-checked failover:** stop returning an IP when its health check fails.
- **Weighted:** send 90% to `v1`, 10% to `v2` for a canary.
- **Geo / latency-based:** return the region nearest the user (covered in the global traffic lesson).

The resolver, not the user, is what the authoritative server sees. If a user in Paris uses a resolver in Virginia, they may be sent to a US region. The **EDNS Client Subnet** extension lets resolvers pass along part of the client's IP (for example a /24) to fix this, at some cost to privacy and cache efficiency.

> [!tip] Where DNS load balancing fits
> DNS is great for coarse, global decisions: which region, which data centre. Inside a data centre, use a real load balancer, which reacts in seconds and balances per connection or per request.

## DNS as a single point of failure

If your authoritative DNS is unreachable, clients without usable cached or serve-stale answers cannot resolve your names, even if every server is healthy. In October 2016, a DDoS on Dyn made Twitter, GitHub, Netflix and others unreachable for many users.

Mitigations:

- Use a provider with a large **anycast** network.
- Consider **two independent DNS providers** (both listed in your `NS` records).
- Don't set TTLs so low that a short DNS outage immediately becomes a full outage.

## Inside your own systems

DNS is also the default service-discovery mechanism inside clusters. In Kubernetes, a normal `orders.prod.svc.cluster.local` Service resolves to a stable virtual IP; routing updates behind it handle changing Pods without a DNS change. Headless Services instead return Pod addresses, so DNS caching matters directly. Long-lived connections can stay attached to an existing backend in either case.

## Key takeaways

- Resolution goes stub → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative, with caching at every level.
- Know `A`, `AAAA`, `CNAME`, `NS`, `MX`, `TXT`, `SRV` and why a CNAME can't sit at the apex.
- TTL is a trade-off between agility and query load; lower it well before a planned change.
- TTLs are often not honoured exactly, so expect a long tail of stale clients.
- DNS can do coarse load balancing and failover, but it's slow to react and sees the resolver, not the user.
- Your DNS provider is a critical dependency; treat it like one.

- [Choosing a routing policy (Amazon Route 53)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy.html)

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver with an empty cache receives a query for `www.example.com`. Which server does it ask first?

options.text: The authoritative server for `example.com`
options.explanation: The resolver doesn't yet know which servers are authoritative for `example.com`; it discovers that from referrals, starting at the root.

options.text: The `.com` TLD server
options.explanation: It needs the root's referral to learn where the `.com` servers are, unless that referral is already cached, which the question rules out.

options.text: The domain's registrar
options.explanation: Registrars publish `NS` records into the TLD zone, but they aren't queried during resolution. The path is root → TLD → authoritative.

options.text: A root server
options.explanation: Correct. With nothing cached, the only thing a resolver knows is the root server addresses (built in as 'root hints'). The root refers it to the `.com` TLD servers.

questions.workedExample:
1. Cold cache: the resolver knows only the root hints.
2. Root replies: "I don't know `www.example.com`, but here are the `.com` servers."
3. `.com` replies: "Here are `example.com`'s name servers (`NS`)."
4. The authoritative server returns the `A` record.
5. The resolver caches **each** answer for its TTL. The next lookup for anything under `.com` can skip the root and go straight to the `.com` servers; the next lookup for anything under `example.com` can go straight to its name servers.

questions.prompt: You want `example.com` (the bare apex) to point at your CDN's hostname `d123.cdn.net`. Why can't you just add `example.com CNAME d123.cdn.net`?

options.text: CNAMEs can only point to IP addresses
options.explanation: It's the other way around: a CNAME always points to another *name*. `A` and `AAAA` records hold IP addresses.

options.text: The apex must hold `SOA` and `NS` records, and a CNAME cannot coexist with the required SOA and NS data at the same name
options.explanation: Correct. The DNS specification says a CNAME cannot coexist with ordinary data such as SOA and NS (DNSSEC-related exceptions do not permit an apex CNAME). Since the apex must have `SOA`/`NS`, an apex CNAME is invalid; providers offer ALIAS/ANAME records as a workaround.

options.text: CNAMEs are not cached, so it would be too slow
options.explanation: CNAME records have TTLs and are cached like any other record. The restriction is about the specification, not performance.

options.text: Browsers refuse to follow CNAMEs on the apex
options.explanation: Browsers don't see record types; the resolver follows CNAMEs for them. The problem is in the DNS zone, not the browser.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every zone apex must have an `SOA` record and `NS` records.
2. RFC rules: if a name has a CNAME, it must have **no other ordinary data**, apart from specified DNSSEC-related records.
3. Both can't be true at `example.com`, so the CNAME is invalid.
4. Fix: use your provider's ALIAS/ANAME (Route 53 alias) record, which resolves `d123.cdn.net` itself and returns plain `A`/`AAAA` records. Or redirect the apex to `www.example.com` and CNAME that.

questions.prompt: `api.example.com` has a TTL of 86,400 s (24 h). On Monday at 09:00 you lower it to 60 s, and at 09:30 you change the `A` record to a new data centre. When can you be reasonably confident almost all well-behaved resolvers are using the new IP?

options.text: From about 09:00 on Tuesday, 24 hours after the TTL was lowered
options.explanation: Correct. A resolver that cached the old record at 08:59 Monday with TTL 86,400 keeps it until about 08:59 Tuesday. Only then is normally expiring caches stop reusing the old long-TTL entry; they re-query when needed, subject to serve-stale policy.

options.text: Around 09:31, one minute after the change
options.explanation: That would be true only if every cache already held the 60 s TTL. Resolvers that cached the record before 09:00 hold it with a 24 h TTL and won't look again until it expires.

options.text: Around 10:30, an hour later
options.explanation: There's nothing special about an hour. Caches populated just before 09:00 keep the old record for up to 24 hours.

options.text: Never, because DNS changes need the registrar to propagate them
options.explanation: Changing an `A` record happens at your authoritative server; the registrar is only involved for `NS` delegation changes. Caches converge as TTLs expire.

questions.workedExample:
1. Worst case: a resolver cached the record at 08:59 with TTL = 86,400 s.
2. Lowering the TTL at 09:00 doesn't reach that cache; it only affects answers given *after* 09:00.
3. That cache keeps the old IP until 08:59 + 24 h = **08:59 Tuesday**.
4. Correct playbook: lower the TTL, **wait the old TTL** (24 h), then make the change. Then caches converge within ~60 s.
5. Even then, keep the old servers up for a while: some clients ignore TTLs.

questions.prompt: You use plain round-robin DNS with three `A` records for `api.example.com`. One server dies. What happens?

options.text: DNS automatically stops returning the dead IP
options.explanation: Plain DNS has no idea whether a server is alive. Health-checked DNS (e.g. Route 53 failover) can do this, but plain round robin keeps returning all three records.

options.text: All traffic fails because DNS needs every server healthy
options.explanation: DNS doesn't check servers at all. Clients given one of the two live IPs succeed normally.

options.text: Traffic is automatically spread over the two remaining servers with no errors
options.explanation: That's what a load balancer with health checks does. DNS round robin has no feedback loop, so errors continue until the record is removed and caches expire.

options.text: Roughly a third of new connection attempts hit the dead IP, and clients that don't retry another address fail until the record is changed and caches expire
options.explanation: Correct. Each resolver keeps handing out the dead IP. Some clients (browsers) try the next address after a timeout; many API clients don't, so they fail.

questions.workedExample:
1. Resolvers return all three IPs in rotating order; clients usually take the first.
2. With one server dead, ~1/3 of fresh lookups put the dead IP first.
3. Browsers implement fallback (try the next IP after a timeout, often seconds); typical HTTP libraries may just fail.
4. Recovery: remove the record (manually or via health checks) **and** wait for TTL expiry.
5. That's why DNS is used for coarse routing, with a health-checking load balancer behind each IP.

questions.prompt: Your DNS failover is configured with a 30 s TTL, yet after a region fails, 5% of traffic keeps hitting the dead region for over an hour. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some clients cache DNS results far longer than the TTL (e.g. an old JVM caching forever)
options.explanation: Correct. Java historically cached successful lookups indefinitely when a security manager was installed, and many SDKs and apps cache at startup. They never ask again.

options.text: Long-lived connections (connection pools, HTTP/2, WebSockets) never re-resolve while the connection stays open
options.explanation: Correct. DNS is consulted only when a new connection is opened. A pooled connection to a now-broken region may hang or fail slowly instead of moving.

options.text: Some resolvers enforce a minimum TTL higher than 30 s
options.explanation: Correct. Some ISP resolvers clamp low TTLs up to several minutes or more to reduce load, so they serve the stale answer longer.

options.text: UDP packets are slower than TCP, so the new answer takes longer to arrive
options.explanation: UDP is if anything faster (no handshake). Transport speed affects milliseconds per query, not hour-long staleness.

questions.workedExample:
Think about where the old answer can still live:

1. **Client caches** that ignore TTL (JVM `networkaddress.cache.ttl`, apps that resolve once).
2. **Open connections**, which bypass DNS entirely until they close.
3. **Resolvers clamping TTLs** to a minimum.

UDP vs TCP speed is irrelevant. Mitigations: configure client DNS caching, set a max connection lifetime on pools (e.g. 5 min) so they re-resolve, and fail fast on errors so clients reconnect.

questions.prompt: You use geo-based DNS to send European users to `eu-west` and US users to `us-east`. Analytics show many users in Germany are being routed to `us-east`. They all use a large public resolver. What's the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: German ISPs block European IP ranges
options.explanation: There's no such blocking. The users aren't failing to reach Europe; DNS is choosing the wrong region for them.

options.text: The `A` record TTL is too long
options.explanation: A long TTL slows changes, but it doesn't cause the wrong region to be chosen in the first place. The selection uses the resolver's location.

options.text: The public resolver's query reaches your authoritative server from a US-located IP, so geo-DNS sees the resolver's location. Support EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) so you see the client's subnet.
options.explanation: Correct. Authoritative servers only see the resolver's address. ECS lets the resolver include a truncated client subnet, so the geo decision uses the user's real network.

options.text: Geo-DNS only works with IPv6
options.explanation: Geo-DNS works on IPv4 and IPv6 equally. The problem is whose IP the geolocation is based on.

questions.workedExample:
1. Geo-DNS decides based on **the IP that sent the query**, which is the recursive resolver, not the user.
2. If the resolver's egress appears to be in the US (or its anycast routing lands the query at a US site), users get the US answer.
3. **ECS** adds e.g. the client's /24 to the query, so the authoritative server can geolocate the user.
4. Trade-offs: ECS leaks some client information and fragments resolver caches (one entry per subnet), so not every resolver sends it.
5. Alternative fix: anycast at the network layer, which routes by where the user's packets actually enter.

questions.prompt: You're designing DNS for a service that must stay reachable even if your DNS provider suffers a large DDoS like the 2016 Dyn attack. Which approach most directly addresses that risk?

options.text: Lower all TTLs to 5 seconds so you can react faster
options.explanation: This makes things worse: when the provider is down, caches expire within seconds and every client immediately fails to resolve. Longer TTLs actually ride out short DNS outages.

options.text: Host the zone on two independent authoritative providers and list both sets of name servers in your `NS` records
options.explanation: Correct. Resolvers try the other `NS` set if one doesn't answer, so an attack on one provider doesn't take you offline. You must keep the zones in sync (via zone transfers or automation).

options.text: Put the website behind a CDN
options.explanation: A CDN protects your origin servers, but users still need DNS to find the CDN. If the DNS provider is down, they can't resolve the name at all.

options.text: Use DNS over HTTPS
options.explanation: DoH protects the privacy of the client–resolver hop. It does nothing if the authoritative servers can't answer.

questions.workedExample:
1. The failure is: **authoritative servers unreachable**.
2. Once cached records expire, clients without usable serve-stale data cannot resolve the name, however healthy your servers are.
3. Redundancy at that layer = **multiple providers**: e.g. `NS` records for both `ns1.provider-a.net` and `ns1.provider-b.net`.
4. Supporting moves: moderate TTLs (minutes to hours for stable records) so caches bridge short outages.
5. Cost: keeping two providers' zones in sync, and advanced features (geo, health checks) may differ between them.

questions.prompt: A developer runs `dig new.example.com` before the record exists, then creates it. The zone's `SOA` record has a TTL of 900 s and a `MINIMUM` field of 3,600 s. For roughly how long might the resolver they used keep saying the name doesn't exist?

options.text: Up to about 15 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. Under RFC 2308 the negative-caching TTL is the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and its MINIMUM field: min(900, 3,600) = 900 s.

options.text: Up to about an hour
options.explanation: That uses the MINIMUM field alone. RFC 2308 caps the negative TTL at the SOA record's own TTL as well, so the smaller value wins.

options.text: Not at all, because negative answers are never cached
options.explanation: They are cached, precisely to stop repeated lookups for non-existent names hammering authoritative servers.

options.text: Until the registrar propagates the change, usually 24 to 48 hours
options.explanation: Adding a record happens on your authoritative servers; the registrar isn't involved. The '48 hours to propagate' folklore is really just TTLs expiring.

questions.workedExample:
1. The `NXDOMAIN` response includes the zone's `SOA` record.
2. RFC 2308: negative TTL = min(SOA TTL, SOA MINIMUM) = min(900, 3,600) = **900 s**.
3. So that resolver may answer 'doesn't exist' for up to 15 minutes after the record is created.
4. Other resolvers that never cached the miss see the new record immediately.
5. Lesson: create records *before* anything starts querying them, or keep the negative TTL short.

link.title: RFC 2308: Negative caching of DNS queries

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver fetched `api.example.com` (TTL 300 s) from the authoritative server at 10:00:00. A laptop asks that resolver for the name at 10:04:00. What TTL does the laptop receive, and when does its own cached copy expire?

options.text: 300 s; the laptop's copy expires at 10:09:00
options.explanation: Resolvers don't reset the TTL when they hand out a cached answer. They pass on the time remaining.

options.text: 0 s; the laptop must ask again immediately
options.explanation: The resolver's entry still has 60 s left, so it hands that remaining time on.

options.text: 60 s; the laptop's copy expires at 10:05:00, the same moment as the resolver's
options.explanation: Correct. The TTL counts down in the resolver's cache. Every downstream cache inherits the remaining time, so they all expire together.

options.text: It depends on the laptop's clock, so it can't be known
options.explanation: TTLs are relative durations in seconds, not absolute timestamps, so clock skew doesn't change the result.

questions.workedExample:
1. 10:00:00 the resolver caches the record with 300 s to live → expires at 10:05:00.
2. 10:04:00 the laptop asks: 240 s have passed, so 300 − 240 = **60 s** remain.
3. The resolver answers with TTL 60.
4. The laptop caches it for 60 s → expires at **10:05:00**.

Consequence: after you change a record, the worst-case wait is about one TTL from the most recent fetch of the old answer before the change, not one TTL per layer of caching.

questions.prompt: You add many `TXT` records and enable DNSSEC, so some responses for your domain grow to about 3 KB. Users on a few corporate networks now fail to resolve the name, while everyone else is fine. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.text: The answer no longer fits in the UDP size the client advertised, so the server sets the truncated flag, and the corporate firewall blocks the TCP port 53 retry
options.explanation: Correct. Large answers fall back to TCP. Some firewalls still wrongly allow only UDP 53, so the TCP retry fails.

options.text: Large UDP responses are fragmented at the IP layer, and some middleboxes drop the fragments
options.explanation: Correct. This is why the DNS community settled on advertising around 1,232 bytes (DNS Flag Day 2020): stay under typical path limits and use TCP for anything bigger.

options.text: DNSSEC makes resolvers ignore TTLs
options.explanation: DNSSEC does not tell resolvers to ignore TTLs; validation can further limit use of data by signature validity.

options.text: A CNAME now sits at the zone apex
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario adds a CNAME. Apex CNAMEs are a zone-configuration error that would break resolution for everyone, not only a few networks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Classic DNS assumed 512-byte UDP answers; EDNS(0) lets clients advertise more.
2. If the response is bigger than advertised, the server returns a truncated (TC) reply → the client must retry over **TCP**.
3. Failure path A: TCP/53 blocked → retry fails.
4. Failure path B: a big UDP answer fragments; fragments get dropped → timeout.
5. Fixes: trim records, prefer compact DNSSEC algorithms (ECDSA), and ask affected networks to allow TCP/53 (which RFC 7766 makes mandatory).

questions.prompt: Your apex `example.com` uses your DNS provider's ALIAS record pointing at a CDN hostname, while `www.example.com` is a normal CNAME to the same CDN. The CDN steers users with DNS. Users in Asia report that `example.com` is much slower than `www.example.com`. What's the likely cause?

options.text: ALIAS records are cached for longer than CNAMEs
options.explanation: TTL length affects how quickly changes spread, not which PoP a user gets on a given lookup.

options.text: The apex can't use HTTPS
options.explanation: The apex can use HTTPS like any other name; certificates can cover `example.com` as a SAN.

options.text: Browsers deprioritise apex domains
options.explanation: Browsers don't treat apex names differently when connecting.

options.text: Your DNS provider resolves the CDN's name itself, so the CDN's geo-steering sees the provider's location (perhaps in the US) rather than the user's resolver, and hands back a far-away PoP
options.explanation: Correct. With a CNAME, the user's own resolver queries the CDN, which can pick a nearby PoP. With ALIAS, the lookup happens server-side, so the location signal is lost unless the provider forwards client-subnet information.

questions.workedExample:
1. `www` → CNAME → the user's resolver (in Asia) asks the CDN's DNS → the CDN sees an Asian resolver → returns an Asian PoP.
2. `example.com` → ALIAS → your DNS provider looks up the CDN name *itself*, from its own servers.
3. The CDN sees the DNS provider's address → may return a US or EU PoP → your provider passes those `A` records to the Asian user.
4. Fixes: redirect the apex to `www`, use a provider whose ALIAS integration supports the CDN properly (e.g. Route 53 alias records to CloudFront, or EDNS Client Subnet), or use a CDN with anycast addresses at the apex.

questions.prompt: Your authoritative DNS provider is unreachable for two hours. Your records have a 300 s TTL. You expected everyone to fail after five minutes, but many users kept resolving your name throughout. What most likely explains this?

options.text: Root servers keep a backup copy of every domain's records
options.explanation: Root servers only hold delegations to TLD servers. They never store your `A` records.

options.text: Many recursive resolvers implement serve-stale (RFC 8767), returning expired cached answers when the authoritative servers can't be reached
options.explanation: Correct. Major public resolvers do this deliberately: a slightly stale answer is better than a failure. It cushions DNS outages, though you can't rely on every resolver doing it.

options.text: The TTL was silently raised by the registrar
options.explanation: Registrars don't edit the TTLs of records in your zone.

options.text: Browsers ignore DNS entirely after the first visit
options.explanation: Browsers cache DNS briefly and reuse connections, but they still resolve names when opening new connections; they don't skip DNS for hours.

questions.workedExample:
1. Expected: after 300 s, caches expire → resolvers ask your provider → no answer → failure.
2. Serve-stale changes step 3: if the refresh fails, the resolver keeps serving the expired entry (RFC 8767 suggests a maximum staleness of 1 to 3 days).
3. Users behind such resolvers carry on; users behind strict resolvers fail.
4. Don't design around it: you still want multiple providers. But it explains partial survival and also why some clients see old data longer than the TTL.

lessons.title: TCP vs UDP, and HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
lessons.summary: What TCP and UDP guarantee, how each HTTP version uses connections, and why head-of-line blocking drove the move to QUIC.
lessons.body:
Every HTTP request rides on a transport protocol. The choice of transport, and how HTTP uses it, explains most of the performance differences between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. This lesson builds up from TCP and UDP to the problem each HTTP version was designed to fix.

## TCP: a reliable, ordered byte stream

TCP gives applications the illusion of a reliable pipe:

- **Connection-oriented:** a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) costs 1 RTT before data flows.
- **Reliable:** lost segments are detected and retransmitted.
- **Ordered:** bytes are delivered to the app in the order they were sent.
- **Flow control:** the receiver advertises how much it can buffer.
- **Congestion control:** the sender probes for available bandwidth.

That last point matters for performance. A new TCP connection starts in **slow start**, with a small congestion window (typically 10 segments ≈ 14 KB, proposed by the Experimental RFC 6928; the actual initial window is implementation/configuration dependent). It roughly doubles each RTT until loss appears, after which the sender cuts its window (by half for classic Reno, by about 30% for CUBIC, the Linux default) and grows more cautiously. So a fresh connection can't use a fast link fully for several round trips:

| RTT # | Window | Cumulative sent |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14 KB | 14 KB |
| 2 | 28 KB | 42 KB |
| 3 | 56 KB | 98 KB |
| 4 | 112 KB | 210 KB |

In this idealised round-based model, a 200 KB response needs four transmission rounds, assuming a 14 KB starting window, doubling each round, no loss, immediate ACKs and negligible serialisation. This is not an exact packet-timing model or a bandwidth-independent guarantee. On a 1 Gbps link, 200 KB would take under 2 ms to clock out; at 50 ms RTT, slow start makes it take about 200 ms. **Warm, reused connections are fast; new ones are slow.**

> [!note] TCP Fast Open
> TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413) lets a returning client put data in the SYN, saving the handshake RTT. Deployment depends on both endpoints and middlebox compatibility.

## UDP: just datagrams

UDP is almost nothing on top of IP:

- No handshake, no connection state.
- No retransmission, no ordering, no congestion control.
- Each datagram is independent; it may be lost, duplicated or reordered.

That sounds worse, but it's exactly what some applications want:

| Use | Why UDP |
|---|---|
| DNS | One packet each way; retry is cheap |
| Voice/video calls | A late packet is useless; skip it |
| Games | Latest state matters, not old state |
| QUIC (HTTP/3) | Builds its own reliability in user space |

> [!note] Reliability isn't free
> TCP's ordering guarantee means one lost packet holds back everything after it, even data that arrived fine. That's **head-of-line (HOL) blocking** at the transport layer, and it's the thread that ties this whole lesson together.

## HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection

HTTP/1.1 (first specified in 1997, now RFC 9112) made **persistent connections** (`keep-alive`), so one TCP connection can carry many requests in sequence. But on each connection, a response must finish before the next request's response can start:

```
Conn 1: [req A ][resp A    ][req B][resp B]
Conn 2: [req C ][resp C][req D ][resp D   ]
...up to ~6 connections per origin
```

This is **HTTP-level head-of-line blocking**: a slow response blocks everything queued behind it on that connection. *Pipelining* (sending several requests without waiting) was specified but never worked reliably because responses still had to come back in order, and buggy proxies broke it. Browsers turned it off.

Workarounds from the HTTP/1.1 era:

- Browsers open **~6 parallel connections** per origin.
- Sites used **domain sharding** (`img1.`, `img2.`...) to get more connections.
- **Spriting and concatenation** bundled many small files into one.

All of these add handshakes, slow-start penalties or cache-busting problems.

## HTTP/2: multiplexing over one connection

HTTP/2 (2015, now RFC 9113) keeps HTTP's semantics (methods, headers, status codes) but changes the wire format:

- **Binary framing.** Messages are split into frames.
- **Streams.** Each request/response is a stream with an ID; frames from many streams interleave on **one TCP connection**.
- **HPACK header compression.** Repeated headers (cookies, user agents) are sent as small table references.
- **Prioritisation** hints. The original dependency-tree scheme was complex and inconsistently implemented, and RFC 9113 deprecated it in favour of the simpler *Extensible Priorities* scheme (RFC 9218), which HTTP/3 also uses.

```
One TCP connection:
[A1][B1][C1][A2][C2][B2][A3]...
 A, B, C = streams, interleaved
```

A slow response no longer blocks fast ones, so the HTTP-level HOL problem is solved. The 6-connection limit, sharding and spriting become unnecessary, and often harmful (sharding defeats the single-connection design).

**Server push** was also part of HTTP/2, but it was hard to use well and browsers (Chrome in 2022) removed support. `103 Early Hints` is the replacement.

### The problem HTTP/2 can't fix

All those streams share one TCP byte stream. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back **every byte after it** until the retransmission arrives, even bytes belonging to unrelated streams:

```
Packets: [A1][B1][xx][A2][C2]
               lost ^
TCP delivers A1, B1, then WAITS.
A2 and C2 arrived but are stuck.
```

On a clean network this rarely matters. On lossy mobile or Wi-Fi links (a few per cent loss), HTTP/2 over one connection can perform *worse* than HTTP/1.1 over six, for two reasons:

- A single loss stalls every stream instead of one-sixth of the traffic.
- The one connection's congestion window shrinks on loss, cutting throughput for everything. With six connections, only one window shrinks at a time.

## HTTP/3 and QUIC: fixing transport HOL blocking

HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) runs over **QUIC** (RFC 9000, 2021), a transport built on UDP. QUIC re-implements reliability and congestion control, and it tracks **ordering per stream**:

- A loss of application stream data does not create TCP-style ordering dependencies between otherwise independent streams.
- Other streams keep flowing.

```
QUIC packets: [A1][B1][xx][A2][C2]
                  lost ^ (B2)
A1, A2, C2 delivered at once.
Only stream B waits for B2.
```

Two subtleties. Ordering still holds *within* a stream, so a loss does stall that one stream. And congestion control is still per connection, so loss slows the whole connection's sending rate even though it no longer blocks delivery. HTTP/3 also replaced HPACK with **QPACK**, because HPACK assumes headers arrive in order, which would have reintroduced cross-stream blocking. QPACK bounds and manages header dependencies; it does not eliminate every possible cross-stream dependency.

QUIC brings several other wins:

1. **Combined handshake.** Transport and TLS 1.3 are negotiated together in the same packets: 1 RTT for a new connection instead of TCP's 1 plus TLS's 1, and **0-RTT** for resumption, where the request rides in the very first flight (with replay caveats; see the TLS lesson).
2. **Connection migration.** Nonzero *connection IDs* let endpoints identify connections across changes to the IP/port 4-tuple. A phone can keep its connection when changing networks if migration is supported and permitted; path validation and connection-ID handling still matter.
3. **Always encrypted.** Even most transport headers are encrypted, which stops middleboxes from ossifying the protocol.
4. **User-space implementation.** It can evolve with app releases, not OS kernel upgrades.

Costs and caveats:

- **CPU:** UDP processing in user space has historically cost more CPU than kernel TCP (improving with offloads like GSO).
- **Blocked UDP:** some corporate networks block UDP 443. Browsers fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP.
- **Discovery:** browsers usually learn about HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc` header on an HTTP/2 response, or from a DNS `HTTPS` record, so the first visit is often HTTP/2.
- **Load balancing:** L4 balancers must route by QUIC connection ID, not 4-tuple, or migration breaks.

## Side by side

| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | TCP | QUIC/UDP |
| Concurrency | ~6 conns | Streams, 1 conn | Streams, 1 conn |
| HTTP HOL | Yes | No | No |
| TCP HOL | Per conn | Yes, all streams | No |
| New conn setup | 2 RTT | 2 RTT | 1 RTT |
| Resumed, 0-RTT | 1 RTT | 1 RTT | 0 RTT |

Setup figures assume TLS 1.3 and count round trips before the request can be sent. A full TLS 1.2 handshake adds one more RTT over TCP. With TLS 1.3 0-RTT over TCP, the TCP handshake still has to happen first, which is why it's 1 RTT rather than 0.

## Connection reuse in back-end systems

These lessons apply between your own services too:

- **Pool connections.** Opening a new TCP+TLS connection per request to a database or downstream API adds 2+ RTTs and slow start every time. Keep-alive pools are essential.
- **HTTP/2 between services** (gRPC uses it) gives multiplexing over few connections. But a few long-lived connections can **unbalance an L4 load balancer**, which balances connections, not requests. Use an L7 balancer or client-side balancing.
- **Set a max connection age** so pools pick up DNS changes and spread across new backends.

> [!example] A real migration
> Google’s 2017 QUIC deployment paper reports benefits for Search and YouTube in its measured environment. That historical Google QUIC implementation predates standard IETF QUIC; its results are not a guaranteed HTTP/3 speed-up.
>
> Evidence gap: no reproducible benchmark for this app or your network is provided. Exact performance gains and CPU comparisons are omitted; measure representative workloads.

## Key takeaways

- TCP gives a reliable ordered stream at the cost of a handshake, slow start and transport-level HOL blocking.
- UDP gives raw datagrams; it suits DNS, real-time media and as a base for QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1 suffers HTTP-level HOL blocking, so browsers use ~6 connections per origin.
- HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, but one lost packet stalls all streams.
- HTTP/3 on QUIC makes loss recovery per-stream, merges the TLS handshake, supports 0-RTT and survives network changes.
- Reuse connections everywhere; new connections are expensive.

## Further reading

- [High Performance Browser Networking: HTTP/1.x](https://hpbn.co/http1x/)
- [High Performance Browser Networking: HTTP/2](https://hpbn.co/http2/)
- [Head-of-line blocking (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head-of-line_blocking)
- [RFC 9000: QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
- [The road to QUIC (Cloudflare blog)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-road-to-quic/)

questions.prompt: You're building a multiplayer game that sends each player's position 30 times a second. Why do many such games use UDP rather than TCP for position updates?

options.text: UDP encrypts packets automatically
options.explanation: UDP has no encryption at all. Encryption comes from a layer on top (DTLS, QUIC or the game's own scheme).

options.text: UDP guarantees delivery faster than TCP
options.explanation: UDP guarantees nothing about delivery. It's attractive precisely because it doesn't try to deliver everything.

options.text: TCP can't send more than one message per second
options.explanation: TCP can carry very high message rates. The issue isn't throughput but head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.

options.text: A lost update is superseded 33 ms later, so retransmitting it (and blocking newer updates behind it, as TCP would) only adds lag
options.explanation: Correct. TCP's in-order delivery would hold back fresh positions until a stale one is retransmitted. UDP lets the game drop the stale packet and use the newest state.

questions.workedExample:
1. Updates every 1000 / 30 ≈ **33 ms**.
2. With TCP, if one packet is lost, retransmission takes at least 1 RTT (say 60 ms). Meanwhile the next two updates have arrived but TCP **can't deliver them** until the lost one is filled in.
3. Result: a 60+ ms stutter, all to deliver a position that's already out of date.
4. With UDP, the game just uses the newest packet it has. Important events (a kill, a purchase) can be sent with the game's own lightweight acknowledgements.

questions.prompt: In HTTP/1.1, why did browsers open about six TCP connections per origin?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 closes the connection after every request
options.explanation: HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default (keep-alive). The limit is concurrency on a connection, not reuse.

options.text: Without HTTP/1.1 pipelining, each connection handles one request/response at a time, so parallel fetching needs more connections
options.explanation: Correct. Without working pipelining, a connection waits for each response to finish before the next can be sent; multiple connections are the only way to fetch resources concurrently.

options.text: Servers limited each connection to 100 KB
options.explanation: There's no such per-connection size limit in HTTP/1.1. Connections can carry arbitrarily large responses.

options.text: To provide redundancy in case one TCP connection drops
options.explanation: Redundancy isn't the reason. The six connections are for parallel fetching to work around HTTP-level head-of-line blocking.

questions.workedExample:
1. A page needs, say, 60 resources.
2. On one HTTP/1.1 connection, they come back strictly one after another, each costing at least 1 RTT.
3. At 50 ms RTT: 60 × 50 = 3 s minimum.
4. With 6 connections: ~10 rounds × 50 ms ≈ 0.5 s (plus 5 extra handshakes).
5. HTTP/2 instead multiplexes all 60 on one connection: roughly 1–2 RTTs for requests to go out, limited mainly by bandwidth.

questions.prompt: After moving from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2, your site is faster on office broadband but *slower* for users on a congested mobile network with ~2% packet loss. What best explains this?

options.text: All streams share one TCP connection, so each lost packet stalls every stream until it's retransmitted; with HTTP/1.1, a loss stalled only one of six connections
options.explanation: Correct. This is TCP-level head-of-line blocking. HTTP/2 concentrates everything on one connection, so loss has a bigger blast radius, and every loss shrinks the congestion window that all traffic shares, instead of one of six.

options.text: HTTP/2's binary framing is harder for phones to parse
options.explanation: Parsing binary frames is cheap, cheaper than parsing text HTTP/1.1. CPU cost isn't the explanation for loss-related slowdown.

options.text: HPACK compression fails on mobile networks
options.explanation: HPACK works the same on any network. It saves bytes everywhere; it doesn't make loss worse.

options.text: Mobile networks don't support HTTP/2
options.explanation: HTTP/2 runs inside TLS over TCP; the mobile network just sees encrypted TCP traffic and can't tell the difference.

questions.workedExample:
1. HTTP/2 = many streams, **one** TCP connection.
2. TCP delivers bytes in order. If packet 17 is lost, packets 18–40 wait in the kernel even if they belong to other streams.
3. At 2% loss with ~100 packets in flight, a loss happens almost every RTT, so every stream stalls repeatedly.
4. TCP also cuts its congestion window on loss (by half for Reno, about 30% for CUBIC). With one connection, *all* throughput drops; with six, only one connection's share does.
5. HTTP/3 fixes this with per-stream loss recovery in QUIC.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine advantages of HTTP/3 (QUIC) over HTTP/2 (TCP + TLS)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loss of application-stream data need not block delivery on unrelated streams
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC tracks ordering per stream, so loss on stream A doesn't hold back streams B and C.

options.text: Connections can survive a client's IP address changing, for example Wi-Fi to 4G
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC identifies connections by connection ID rather than the IP/port 4-tuple, so it can migrate when the network changes.

options.text: Transport and TLS handshakes are combined, so a new connection needs 1 RTT instead of 2
options.explanation: Correct. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake, and resumption can use 0-RTT.

options.text: It needs less CPU than TCP on servers
options.explanation: Generally the opposite: QUIC runs in user space with per-packet encryption, and has historically cost more CPU than kernel TCP, though offloads are narrowing the gap.

options.text: It works on every network, because UDP is never blocked
options.explanation: Some enterprise firewalls block or throttle UDP 443. That's why browsers keep an HTTP/2 fallback.

questions.workedExample:
Check each claim against how QUIC works:

1. **Per-stream ordering** → no transport HOL across streams. (yes)
2. **Connection IDs** → migration across networks. (yes)
3. **Integrated TLS 1.3** → 1 RTT new, 0-RTT resume. (yes)
4. CPU: user-space UDP plus encryption per packet → typically *more* CPU. (no)
5. UDP blocking exists → fallback is needed. (no)

questions.prompt: In a simplified round-based model, a fresh TCP/TLS1.3 call has two setup RTTs, then a response window starting at 14 KB and doubling each RTT; ignore handshake bytes growing that window, loss, delayed ACKs and serialisation. RTT is 30 ms and the response is 60 KB. Compare with a warm connection able to send the whole response in one round.

options.text: About 30 ms either way, because bandwidth is high
options.explanation: High bandwidth doesn't help the handshakes or slow start; a new connection can't send 60 KB in one RTT because its window starts at ~14 KB.

options.text: About 60 ms fresh versus 30 ms warm
options.explanation: This counts only one handshake RTT plus one data RTT. It misses TLS (another RTT) and the extra RTTs slow start needs for 60 KB.

options.text: About 300 ms fresh, because TLS needs 4 RTTs
options.explanation: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake, not four. That overestimates the setup cost.

options.text: About 150 ms fresh (2 RTT handshakes + ~3 RTT of slow start), versus about 30 ms warm
options.explanation: Correct. TCP + TLS = 60 ms, then 14 + 28 + 56 KB windows means 3 RTTs (90 ms) to deliver 60 KB. A warm connection with a large window does it in ~1 RTT.

questions.workedExample:
Fresh connection:

| Step | RTTs |
|---|---|
| TCP handshake | 1 |
| TLS 1.3 | 1 |
| Data: 14 KB | 1 |
| Data: +28 KB (42) | 1 |
| Data: +56 KB (98 ≥ 60) | 1 |

5 RTT × 30 ms = **150 ms**. (The request itself goes out with the first data round.)

Warm connection: window already large, so 1 RTT = **30 ms**. Connection pooling gives a 5× speed-up here.
